title: Disaster: Day of Crisis
subtitle: One rescuer faces a very bad day
summary: Disaster: Day of Crisis is Monolith Soft's Wii action adventure following former rescue worker Raymond Bryce through a succession of natural catastrophes and terrorist attacks. body: Disaster: Day of Crisis is Monolith Soft's Wii action adventure following former rescue worker Raymond Bryce through a succession of natural catastrophes and terrorist attacks. Cinematic exploration, driving and shooting sequences place different immediate dangers in his path. Saving civilians gives the spectacle a practical focus beyond simply surviving the next collapse. The Wii Remote and Nunchuk perform actions suited to the current emergency, while the story continually changes the situation around Ray. Its structure resembles an escalating disaster film in which the player must keep finding the next workable response.

Ray's condition depends on more than the damage received in a fight. Strenuous activity drains stamina, while smoke and poisonous fumes affect his lungs. Food and opportunities to breathe fresh air help him recover. Rescuing another person can require moving obstacles, carrying someone to safety or completing a first-aid action before time runs out. These demands connect the large-scale catastrophes with the physical work of a rescuer. Reaching a safe position matters because it provides a chance to restore the condition needed for the next dangerous passage.

Shooting sections use the Remote's pointer to aim, with cover and a zoom mode offering different ways to handle incoming fire. Driving instead uses the controller held sideways and tilted to steer. Other emergencies call for timed inputs or gestures with the Remote and Nunchuk. Rescuing civilians earns Survival Points that improve Ray's abilities, while combat rewards support weapon upgrades. The changing controls give each sequence an immediately recognisable task, moving between the responsibilities of keeping Ray alive, stopping an attacker and helping somebody else escape.
